name: South Park

items.component: Project contains all three loan types

summary_en: South Park is the last of them. A 1972 city planning report on recreation and open space states it flatly: until 1948 the South of Market had three major parks, and of those three only South Park remains — Father Crowley Playground became freeway and the Hall of Justice, and Columbia Square, one of the city's oldest parks, was built over by Bessie Carmichael School after a citywide referendum. The same report warned that as the financial district pushed south and Yerba Buena Center replaced housing with commercial development, the need for open space here would grow rather than shrink, and noted that although funds had once been committed to a replacement park south of Market, none was ever built. The park's own upkeep arrives in small sums: the Open Space Acquisition and Park Renovation Fund lists $50,000 to rehabilitate the play area and replace benches, with plans complete but a local group seeking changes to the project's scope. Its most recent renovation is carried by a single contract — Public Works engaged Bauman Landscape & Construction at $2,940,915. The surrounding blocks appear throughout the record too, as the residential community the planners built recreation policy around, and as the site of the supportive-housing hotels on South Park Street that the city funds separately from the park.

These residents are beginning to 55 seek recreational facilities and services for themselves and their pre-school children. Existing Facilities South Park South Park, built as a residential park in 1854, is the last sizable open space left in South of Market. A pleasant, tree- lined park with a small children's play area, South Park has been plagued with problems of safety and maintenance. Seventy thousand dollars was recently invested in redesign of and improvements to South Park. Improvements, designed in consultation with the South Park community, included barbecue areas and tables, new trees and benches, three new groups of play equipment, a small plaza and stage, drinking fountains and recon touring of the park land. These improvements have gone far to make South Park more useful to residents, but a full-time director for the park is still needed. South Park Community Center South Park Community Center is located immediately adjacent to South Park. Although the Recreation and Park Department does not own South Park Community Center, it conducts successful recreational programs here. The Recreation and Park Department director is a South Park resident, and works at the Center on a part-time basis. The Recreation and Park Department should employ the director full time to conduct programs in the Center and in the park.
